questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose the U.S. because of my heritage. Within the U.S., I wanted to experience the college culture while also staying in a city which has more to offer than just the college

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: A little difficult. I had received all the necessary information, but the amount of information made it difficult to sort through to find the relevant information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We were greeted and provided with all necessary information as well as informed about the office for international students, which was very helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. I stayed at a coop called Laurel, which I was very satisfied with. I started looking several months before my exchange semester which made it easy to get a room at the coop. They have all the relevant information on their website.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off campus was great for me, but the coop was located very close to campus, which was also very convenient. Austin is a rather spread out city, so make sure to look up the distance between the place you intend to stay and campus/downtown.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We were provided with information from the office for international students. You choose the courses you want and then you prioritise these courses. They are not allowed to overlap.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I found it to be a pretty easy process, but you can always ask the office for international students for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successful. I got four very interesting courses and I only had classes from monday to Wednesday.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Spend some time looking through the course catalog beforehand so you have an idea which courses you are interested in. Also, spend some time thinking about the course composition that you want - classes are not allowed to overlap, so you can try to use a calendar to out together different class schedules depending on which courses you end up getting. Also, there is quite a large difference between professors, so ask around about other people's experiences with professors.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I thought the level was very fitting. It varied depending on the course and professor, but I found it to be well balanced between easy enough to follow along without too much time spent preparing but also challenging enough that I ended up learning quite a lot.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In the US in general, they are very fond of the socratic method, whereby the professors ask students questions in order to arrive at an answer to a legal issue, even if the student does not raise their hand. It can seem intimidating, but I found it to be quite enjoyable. I didn't spend too much time preparing for classes, but I still felt prepared for questions. Also, it varies from professor to professor how much they use this method of teaching, so I wouldn't be worried about it.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: U.S. law, an introduction (professor Haynes), Business Associations (professor Damman), Negotiation (professor Jury) and Venture Transactions (professor Vela)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed all the courses. U.S law was a good and rather light introduction to the U.S. legal system. Business Associations with professor Damman was one of the most rewarding courses I have had, as you learn an incredible amount about U.S. corporate law, M&A, economic theory and business acumen. Negotiation with professor Jury was not a very legal-heavy course, but Jury created a very comfortable atmosphere with fun exercises throughout the course. Venture Transactions with Vela is the best course I have had during my time as a law student. It was definitely challenging, but I learned so much about venture capital since the course encompassed both general concepts within venture, fund structure, tax benefits, negotiation, math in relation to ownership stakes through different financing rounds and in-depth analysis of the contracts used within venture capital.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing too unexpected, mostly just travelling and cultural experiences. You can always adjust the amount you spend on this based on your available finances though.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing was very expensive. The coop was one of the cheapest housing options I could find in Austin but I still came out to more than DKK 8.000 pr. month. However, food was included in the rent, so this was cheaper than I expected for me.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are endless opportunities for cultural, athletic and social activities through UT. There are multiple gyms, pools, indoor tracks, basketball courts, volleyball courts etc. available to students for free. Other than that, there are a ton of athletic clubs within different sports that you can join. This is the case for other types of cultural and social activities as well. I would highly recommend making use of some of these opportunities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: College sports are a huge part of college life, especially college football. I would highly recommend getting the big ticket and going to some of the college football games, basketball games, volleyball games etc. Austin nightlife is also very fun, so I would recommend going out quite a bit as well to experience this.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I enjoy going out, so I would recommend experiencing Austins nightlife or spending time canoeing on lady bird lake,  Other than that, the U.S. has plenty of destinations to visit for weekend or holiday trips, especially if you are willing to travel a bit to destinations such as New Orleans, Nashville, California etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The culture is different, but in a way that is easy to adjust to for Europeans.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Say yes to as many things as you can in the beginning. I found some of my closest friends during the first day in Austin because someone suggested that the exchange students in the law school go out to dinner. I also found some very good friends at the coop, so think about placing yourself in as many situations as you can where you get to meet other people, whether it be through your living situation, classes, exchange program, sports programs etc.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None. I enjoyed the american culture quite a bit. People are very open and friendly - it takes some getting used to, but it is also a very welcome change when you are looking for friends.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness amongst americans and the focus on enjoying yourself and having a good time. There was such a great atmosphere and an interest in meeting new people, which is exactly what you want as an exchange student.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Find some good friends as soon as possible, they were without a doubt the most important part of my exchange.
2. Bring as much money as you can through your own savings and through grants - even if you don't intend on spending it all, it is always great to have the opportunity to go travelling or go out with friends without having to worry about your finances.
3. Make a list of all the things you want to do during your exchange, such as local attractions and travel destinations. Be realistic though, because a big part of being on exchange is just enjoying life in a new city, so you want to find a good balance between spending your time on trips and attractions and spending your time getting to know the city and being with friends.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Start as early as you can with all the requirements for your exchange, such as TOEFL tests, visa applications etc. Especially the TOEFL test was quite expensive and not as easy as one might think, and the deadline for when you have to document having taken the test is very early, so you need to start this process early so you don't end up missing the deadline.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friendships I made during the semester, having a more chill semester where enjoying life was more important than studying and creating a bond to a new city.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: All the hours spent preparing. It was worth it though - the more you prepare, the less you have to worry about when you arrive, leaving more time to enjoy your exchange.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
